«С тех пор как Эрстед открыл, что магнит: "Since Ørsted discovered that magnetic actions are caused not only by permanent magnets but also by electric currents, there have seemed to be two completely independent ways of creating a magnetic field. This situation led to the desire to consider the difference in the nature of these two sources of the field as only apparent and encouraged attempts to explain the magnetic field excitation by a single cause. Soon after Ørsted’s discovery, Ampère proposed his famous hypothesis of molecular currents, which explained the magnetic properties (of paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances) by currents circulating in molecules. Similarly, the electron theory, especially in the form given by H. A. Lorentz—needing a unified understanding of the origin of electromagnetic fields—mainly adhered to Ampère’s hypothesis. But according to this theory, molecular currents, like all electric currents, were created by moving elementary charges. Although these ideas about circulating elementary charges in atoms and molecules (mostly thought of as negative electrons) allowed a unified cause for the origin of electromagnetic fields, they still raised very serious fundamental doubts." Изменение характера намагничивания с мол: The change in the nature of magnetization from the molecular point of view is described quite simply: when an external magnetic field is applied, the elementary magnetic moments of each atom in the body tend to align along the direction of the magnetic field. The rearrangement of this system leads to a change in the angular momentum of each electron in the system. However, the total angular momentum of the body must remain unchanged. Therefore, when the direction of the external magnetic field changes due to the "flip" of magnetic moments, and thus of the angular momenta of electrons related by the gyromagnetic ratio, the magnetized sample as a whole will start to rotate, which can be detected, for example, by the deflection of a light beam reflected from a mirror attached to the sample under study.
